title: Neighbors
hookLine: footsteps through the ceiling, and why the Metta Sutta names the near and the unseen
tomorrow: keep the old ways, or change them? a temple meeting gets loud.

lines: SEEN AND UNSEEN, FAR AND NEAR.
cards: The neighbor upstairs drops something heavy just before midnight. You know their footsteps, their dog's bark, the hour their alarm goes off. You may not know their name.
Now an odd detail in the Metta Sutta, the Buddha's teaching on loving-kindness. It wishes well to all beings, which should cover it.
But it keeps going and lists them: the weak and the strong, the big and the small, the seen and the unseen, those living far off and those living near. Why spell it out? Isn't all enough?

teach.b: Here's one way to solve it, and it starts with how wishes work. All is easy. You can wish the whole world well without picturing a single face.

teach.h: THE LIST GIVES THE WISH A PLACE.
teach.b: The list slows you down and makes you look at actual beings, one kind at a time, so the wish has somewhere to land. And two items on that list fit a neighbor exactly. The near: those living close by.
Kindness to the far-off is a lovely idea; kindness to the person whose music comes through your wall at night is practice.
The near is where metta gets tested, because the near can annoy you.
Then the unseen. Neighbors are often half-seen: a car in the driveway, a light in the window, a name on a mailbox. The sutta reaches past what you can see, so a person you only hear still counts.
The verse right before the list sets the tone: may all beings be happy and at ease.
Then the list keeps that wish from floating off into the sky, and walks it to the house next door. Later in the same short text comes the well-known picture of a mother protecting her only child.
That's the size of the care it asks for. The near ones are where you start.

how: The Metta Sutta is chanted in Buddhist temples and homes; in loving-kindness practice, some people move outward from themselves to the people physically nearest them, then further.

o: people you have to like because they live close by
the near, half-seen people where a wish for all gets an address
strangers you can safely ignore, since they're private

games.q: the Metta Sutta's list — tap the pairs.
p: easy to wish without a single face
a mother and her only child
the size of the care it asks for

s: the Metta Sutta wishes well to all beings and stops there
it goes on to list them: weak and strong, seen and unseen, far and near.
the Metta Sutta includes beings living near as well as far
both are on its list, so the wish reaches the house next door.
loving-kindness is meant for people you already like
the list includes the near, who can annoy you, and the unseen, whom you barely know.

games.q: a new neighbor's car blocks your driveway for the second morning. you've never met them. what's the Metta Sutta's way in?
o: leave an anonymous note on the windshield so you don't have to talk.
knock, say your name, ask about the car, and welcome them to the street.
say nothing and wish them well silently; metta is only an inner practice.
games.why: the near ones are where the wish gets an address. meeting them turns an unseen neighbor into a seen one.

practice: Picture the doors nearest yours: across the hall, upstairs, next door, down the street. Go to each one in your mind and rest there a breath, even at the door you know least, or the one that annoys you most.
With each, offer the Metta Sutta's plain wish: may you be happy and at ease, whoever you are.

wordCard.voice: Neighbors: in the Metta Sutta's list, the near and the half-seen, where a wish for all beings gets an address.

carryVoice: Here's the line: next door is where all beings starts. Four of six on friends and community.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8 (Karaniya Metta Sutta: may all beings be happy and at ease; whether weak or strong, long or short, seen or unseen, living far or near, born or seeking birth; as a mother would protect her only child)
